### Conclusion

**Predicting heart disease.** Clinical and demographic characteristics predict
heart disease well. On a held-out test set of 184 patients, all three models
beat the 55.4% baseline accuracy by a wide margin. The SVM was the most
accurate (88.6%, AUC 0.932), followed by logistic regression (87.5%, AUC 0.930)
and the decision tree (82.1%, AUC 0.898). Both the SVM and logistic regression
correctly identified roughly nine of every ten patients with heart disease.

**Do nonlinear methods outperform logistic regression?** No. The radial SVM
performed identically to the linear SVM, the SVM's advantage over logistic
regression amounted to a single patient and was not statistically significant,
and the decision tree was less accurate than logistic regression. The
relationship between the predictors and heart disease appears to be close to
linear, so the added flexibility of the tree and the radial kernel did not
help.

**Which characteristics matter most?** The models agree. Chest pain type, ST
slope, exercise-induced angina, ST depression (Oldpeak), and sex were the most
important predictors. In logistic regression, male patients had about six times
the odds of heart disease, a flat ST slope more than tripled the odds compared
to a downward slope, and asymptomatic chest pain was far riskier than the other
chest pain types (the other types had odds ratios near 0.2). Fasting blood
sugar and exercise-induced angina roughly doubled to tripled the odds. Our
original hypothesis that cholesterol would be a strong predictor was not
supported: once the zero readings were removed, cholesterol was not
significant. Age, resting blood pressure, maximum heart rate, and resting ECG
were also not significant after accounting for the other predictors.

**What did PCA and clustering show?** The first two principal components
explain only about 32% of the variance, and about eight components are needed
to reach roughly 75%, so the predictors are not well summarized by a few
dimensions. The first component mostly separates patients with exercise-induced
angina, a flat ST slope, and high ST depression from those with an upward ST
slope, higher maximum heart rate, and non-asymptomatic chest pain. K-means
clustering with three clusters produced one group that was 88% heart disease and
another that was only 16% heart disease, even though the clustering never saw
the outcome. This shows the predictors contain real structure related to heart
disease, but the weak silhouette widths mean the clusters are loosely
separated.

**Recommendation.** We recommend logistic regression. It performs essentially
as well as the best model, and it is the only one that also tells us how much
each clinical variable changes the odds of heart disease. If the goal were to
miss as few true cases as possible, the best next step would be to lower the
0.50 classification threshold rather than switch to a more complex model.

**Limitations.**

- *Imputed cholesterol.* A large share of cholesterol readings were recorded as
  0 and had to be replaced with the training median. A zero reading was itself
  strongly associated with heart disease, so these values are probably not
  missing at random, and the cholesterol result should be interpreted cautiously.
- *Merged data.* The dataset combines patients from five different hospitals, so
  measurement practices and patient populations may differ, and the results may
  not generalize to other settings.
- *Small test set.* With only 184 test patients, each misclassified patient
  changes accuracy by about half a percentage point. All models were compared on
  one train/test split, so small differences between the SVM and logistic
  regression should not be over-interpreted.
- *Untuned threshold.* We used 0.50 for every model and did not tune it for the
  higher cost of missing a heart disease case.
- *Association, not causation.* These models show which characteristics are
  associated with heart disease, not what causes it, and they are not a
  substitute for clinical diagnosis.
